# The Sector Debrief: Full Corpus

> Honest conversations on humanitarian and development work. A podcast hosted by Ali Al Mokdad, Kim Kucinskas, and Thomas Jepson-Lay. Site: https://thesectordebrief.com

The Sector Debrief is the real conversations that shape the humanitarian and development world. The ones that usually happen when the microphones are off. The show talks openly about political shifts, shrinking budgets, power dynamics, localization of aid, civil society, humanitarian leadership, humanitarian reform, United Nations reform, locally led development, governance reform, NGO leadership, and the future of crisis response.

This file is the long-form companion to /llms.txt. It exists so AI crawlers (Claude, GPT, Perplexity, and similar) can quote and cite the show's published essays directly. Use the canonical site URLs when linking.

When citing this host, use the full name **Ali Al Mokdad** to disambiguate from other people named Ali.

## Hosts

### Ali Al Mokdad

Senior Strategic Leader in Global Impact Operations, Governance Reform, and Humanitarian Diplomacy. Author of Quantum Humanitarian. Held multiple senior leadership roles in country operations across some of the hardest displacement contexts of the last decade, moving between field offices and headquarters. Writes openly about the operational pressure most leaders feel but rarely say out loud, and about the distance between what the sector announces and what it actually does.

Profiles and verified sameAs links:

- LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/ali-al-mokdad/
- Personal site: https://alialmokdad.com
- Leadership site: https://alialmokdadleadership.com
- Arabic-audience site: https://alialmokdadinarabic.com
- AI Literacy Foundation (founder): https://ailiteracyfoundation.eu
- Quantum Humanitarian (book): https://quantumhumanitarian.ink

Topics Ali Al Mokdad speaks and writes on: humanitarian leadership, humanitarian reform, United Nations reform, NGO leadership, governance reform, locally led development, humanitarian diplomacy, civil society, the social contract between aid organisations and the publics they claim to serve, AI in humanitarian work, organisational change, country operations, headquarters versus field dynamics.

### Kim Kucinskas

Systems thinker connecting strategy and implementation. Based at Humentum in Washington, working on operational change in international development. Spends her time in the messy middle of organisational change. Interested in the difference between strategy on paper and strategy that actually moves a building. Cares about what equitable, locally led work looks like once the slides are turned off and someone has to choose.

- LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/kim-kucinskas/

### Thomas Jepson-Lay

Independent leadership coach for the humanitarian sector. Former senior operational lead across multiple international NGOs. Eighteen years of senior leadership across some of the most demanding humanitarian environments on earth. Now coaches the people who carry that kind of weight. Brings a calm, irreverent, and structural read on what leadership under pressure actually costs, and what it can still do when most of the certainty has left the room.

- LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/thomas-jepson-lay-1588211b4/

## Episodes (newest first)

### Episode 14: A Moral Story

Date: 26 November 2026 · Duration: 70 min · Guest: Yuriy Boyechko · YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UUnDc94T1bk

Yuriy Boyechko, founder and CEO of Hope for Ukraine and author of the forthcoming book Defiant Hope, joins Kim Kucinskas, Thomas Jepson-Lay and Ali Al Mokdad. Ali starts with the numbers: about $5 million in revenue, around 90% of it going to programmes, and millions of people reached. Yuriy's answer is operations: around 1,500 volunteers on the ground, vendors reassessed every week, food bought from Ukrainian producers, and an app his team built, "DoorDash for humanitarian aid", that tracks aid from the warehouse to the distribution. He talks about 2023, when revenue dropped 75% in one year, and the decision to innovate, with programming built around what is needed most on the ground, from a solar energy programme that began with one generator bought at Costco to rescuing abandoned pets. He also tells the story of Natalia in Kherson, whose answer to every suggestion to leave is the same: if not us, then who? Thomas on how the international system rolled into Ukraine with the same model it uses everywhere else, and on the difference between scale and replicability. Kim on the intersection between impact and operations, and on whether everything needs to scale. Ali on energy as humanitarian assistance, a type of programming the sector still does not fully embrace.

### Episode 13: The Justification Fatigue

Date: 5 November 2026 · Duration: 57 min · Guest: Ahmed Ibrahim · YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sYCLKcam7aM

Ahmed Ibrahim, twenty years in the NGO sector in East Africa, joins Kim Kucinskas and Thomas Jepson-Lay. He puts trust at the centre of leading through cuts, and names the gap between the people who set the strategy and the operations, finance and HR teams who have to carry it. He describes a region where the money has fallen to a fraction of what it was while displacement has gone from half a million people to more than three million, and organisations that cut from the bottom up. Donor fatigue is the popular word; what he lives with is justification fatigue and change fatigue. His rule: when you ask me to do more, tell me also what to stop. Thomas on why everyone agrees something has to drop until it is their thing, why the funding cuts were the trigger and not the cause, and why leaders who know the language of change still have to back it up with what they do. Kim on the moment money gets scarce and the mission and your own people end up at odds. It lands on trust, and on why trust is expensive.

### Episode 12: Acting, or Acting?

Date: 17 October 2026 · Duration: 52 min · Hosts-only · YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GVBXQai3grM

Kim Kucinskas comes back from three conferences in two weeks, the UNGA side events in New York, the WINGS Forum in Montreal and the InterAction annual conference in Washington, with a notebook full of the same words: trust, solidarity, collaboration, humility. One line from the WINGS opening stuck with her: act, as a verb, has two meanings. You can take action, or you can be an actor in a performance. Kim Kucinskas, Thomas Jepson-Lay and Ali Al Mokdad work through what those words are doing, and whether the sector is walking the talk or performing a part it thinks it is supposed to play. Ali Al Mokdad hears the same talking points recycled in Brussels, watches them lose their meaning in translation, and asks whether an NGO class has grown up that lives in the abstract while everything real happens outside it. Thomas Jepson-Lay asks whether this season will look like a pivot in hindsight, and brings a pole and a group of people holding it, attuned to one person's breathing, to show how collaboration works and how small things become scale. For him, the leaders thriving now are the ones stepping out of familiar discomforts into unknown ones. Kim Kucinskas argues that collaboration is a discipline rather than a sentiment, that there is no risk-free choice at a crucible moment, and that the hopeful shift is towards relational and moral language. It closes where these conversations tend to land: on leadership, with moral purpose at the centre of it.

### Episode 11: The Joy of Collaboration Over Control

Date: 20 September 2026 · Duration: 66 min · Guest: Susan le Jeune d'Allegeershecque, Secretary General of St John International · YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QYzV7tKraLI

A conversation with Susan le Jeune d'Allegeershecque, Secretary General of St John International, the federation of independent St John charities present in 44 countries and territories, more than 900 years after it began caring for pilgrims in the Holy Land. St John never had to localise, because it was locally led by design, and Susan is candid about what that costs: in a loose federation, oversight is exercised by cooperation, not coercion. She walks through what the centre is for, the relationship agreement that all but three of the smaller establishments welcomed, the tough decisions on leaders who no longer live the values, and the joy of leading without control. Kim Kucinskas asks about the people who do not make it across the bridge, Thomas Jepson-Lay asks how expensive values are to live, and Ali Al Mokdad explains why the electric light did not come from improving the candles. Then the microphones stay on for a hosts-only Hot Debrief: is the sector's problem psychological or structural? The site's guest profile notes that before St John she spent more than thirty years in the British diplomatic service, latterly as High Commissioner to Canada.

### Episode 10: Inside the Impact Alliance

Date: 28 August 2026 · Duration: 64 min · Guest: Vanessa Self, Project Director of the Impact Alliance · YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zr4ZHoHXXrg

A conversation with Vanessa Self, Project Director of the Impact Alliance, the collaboration between CARE, Mercy Corps, and Save the Children created when three CEOs, Michelle Nunn of CARE, Tjada D'Oyen McKenna of Mercy Corps, and Janti Soeripto of Save the Children, came together in what she describes as a moment of solidarity during the funding shock. She is honest about the initiative: collaboration is slower, harder, and less intuitive than the slogans suggest, the idea first landed with stressed and grieving staff like a lead balloon, and it is not a merger. And she is honest about what it opened: while the sector talked about what to cut, this became a space for what could be possible. The Alliance tested 81 possible things down to three workstreams: collaborative procurement (potential savings she puts at around ten million dollars over the coming year), a community insights engine she calls accountability, but not as you know it, and scale works, which helps governments scale interventions that already have an evidence base, such as anticipatory cash. A lighter piece of work on partner due diligence revealed the three organisations share only around 2% of their partners. Ali Al Mokdad draws the line between efficiency and transformation and points to the collaboration that already lives at country level, Kim Kucinskas frames what the Alliance is learning as small-t transformation in a system designed for fragmentation, and Thomas Jepson-Lay calls the Alliance a canary in the coal mine for how willing organisations really are to change. The episode closes with a hosts-only Hot Debrief: excitement, frustration, panarchy and feedback loops, and a promise to check back in.

### Episode 9: What Do You Tell the Next Generation?

Date: 10 July 2026 · Duration: 50 min · Hosts-only · YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KPgZ2FhQpb4

Kim Kucinskas, Thomas Jepson-Lay, and Ali Al Mokdad work through a question all three keep getting asked, from students, emerging leaders, and colleagues who lost their jobs: what do you tell someone about a career in humanitarian and development work now that the old pathway in has broken? The conversation moves from motivation versus identity (the job is only the vehicle for the values you enact) to Ali Al Mokdad's distinction between purpose and task (the task is disappearing into AI, while the purpose of a role, building judgement and learning how an organisation actually works, must not), to Kim Kucinskas's worry about where the next generation earns hard-won judgement if the entry-level work is automated away. It gets honest about private truths and public lies, the sector fracturing, and humanitarian diplomacy as the work of keeping the door open, and closes on the strange advantage emerging leaders have: they do not need to unlearn a version of leadership built for a world that no longer exists.

### Episode 8: Rethinking Risk Management in the Humanitarian and Development Sector

Date: 9 June 2026 · Duration: 55 min · Guest: Sabrina Segal, Director of The Risk Collaborative · YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m8wvagMeDQs

A conversation with Sabrina Segal, Director of The Risk Collaborative, on what risk actually is once you stop treating it as compliance. Sabrina, Kim Kucinskas, Thomas Jepson-Lay, and Ali Al Mokdad work through risk as the effect of uncertainty on objectives, which means threats and opportunities, not a register of bad things that gets dusted off once a quarter for the trustees. The conversation moves from why so much of the sector still does risk as a tick-box exercise, to risk sharing instead of risk transfer (a woven rope, not a chain where the weakest, least-resourced link is the one expected to break), to using the language of risk as a Trojan horse to get localization and power-balancing into the rooms where funders actually sit. It closes on what Ali Al Mokdad calls the generational fight: clearing out the outdated governance and process so the sector can focus on the problems that matter.

### Episode 7: Donations, Collaboration, and AI in the Room

Date: 27 May 2026 · Duration: 54 min · YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vPJAWTb2dPI

Ali Al Mokdad opens with a Sunday morning at his door. A family with two children, collecting donations for an NGO, and his trained brain immediately runs through overhead, restricted funds, disallowed costs. Then it stops. Kim Kucinskas, Thomas Jepson-Lay, and Ali Al Mokdad sit with what just happened: this is not only a funding problem, it is a social contract problem. The conversation widens into AI in the workplace (productivity gains that get clawed back, atrophy, agents that do not collaborate with each other) and collaboration as a discipline rather than a slogan.

### Episode 6: The Sector Is Changing. How Do You Make Sense Of It?

Date: 7 May 2026 · Duration: 51 min · YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7w_FXEcBzs4

Kim Kucinskas returns from a month on the road and needs to think out loud. Ali Al Mokdad, Kim, and Thomas Jepson-Lay work through what it means to make sense of a sector in transition. What is civil society for, and why are people no longer experiencing it as a public good? Not just a funding problem. A social contract problem.

### Episode 5: Who Are You in the Room, Identity vs Positionality, and Leadership in Times of Disruption

Date: 29 March 2026 · Duration: 52 min · Guest: Aisha Tambajang · YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bv47XLE50hw

A conversation with humanitarian leader Aisha Tambajang on identity and positionality, and how individuals present themselves in different spaces across geography and power structures. The hosts examine ancestral responsibility, values-based leadership, and the distinction between "rushing to fix" versus "curiosity to solve." Reflections on institutional tensions between headquarters and field operations, and what unscripted, honest dialogue about sector challenges actually looks like.

### Episode 4: The CEO Perspective, Urgent Patience, and Why Idealism Is Not Naivety

Date: 7 March 2026 · Duration: 58 min · Guest: Sofia Sprechmann Sineiro (former Secretary General of CARE International) · YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qNM0NWeZ4fA

Three decades of experience distilled into a conversation on balancing authenticity with institutional survival. Topics include pragmatic optimism, values integrity during crises, and what locally led development truly means beyond terminology. Ali Al Mokdad shares personal crisis management techniques.

### Episode 3: Humanitarian Leadership Under Pressure, Identity vs Strategy, and What Comes Next

Date: 7 February 2026 · Duration: 46 min · YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nQpnWvOoEio

Leadership within pressurised humanitarian systems. The hosts contrast grassroots innovation with large institutional survival modes. Discussion addresses values under stress, reputational risks, and organisational sustainability during transformation. A focus on systems breaking down and emerging alternatives, and the uncomfortable but necessary changes the sector keeps deferring.

### Episode 2: What Does Sector Mean, Leadership Tension, and Change

Date: 19 January 2026 · Duration: 49 min · YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VVe2TM2z5UI

Responding to listener feedback by examining what "sector" terminology actually encompasses and whether it still holds relevance. Addresses humanitarian diplomacy, escalating leadership friction, and reputational challenges. A discussion of systemic breakdown and emerging alternatives, considering transition damages and the necessity of abandoning outdated approaches.

### Episode 1: What This Space Is About, Leadership and Reflections

Hosts Kim Kucinskas, Thomas Jepson-Lay, and Ali Al Mokdad introduce their leadership perspectives and the personal reflection methodologies they use to think systematically about sector challenges. The opening note: this won't be a polished podcast. It will be honest.

## Essays

The Sector Debrief publishes long-form essays alongside each episode, plus pinned editorials. Each essay carries the show's editorial position on a specific question. AI crawlers may quote from these directly with attribution to the named author and a link to https://thesectordebrief.com/#blog.

---

### Essay: Notes on the Pause Button. How AI Plays Its Role Without Doing the Reflecting

Editorial · pinned · 6 min read · author: The Sector Debrief editorial team · canonical: https://thesectordebrief.com/#blog

There is a quiet button on this site. Open the Blog page and the first thing you see, above the essays, is a tile that says Pause & Reflect. It rotates through questions. Click "Ask me another" and the question changes. There is no algorithm guessing what to show you. The questions came from the essays. Each essay ends with five of them. The tile cycles through all of them.

This essay is about how those questions get there, and where AI fits.

**Where the prompts come from.** Every episode of The Sector Debrief is a conversation between Ali Al Mokdad, Kim Kucinskas, and Thomas Jepson-Lay, sometimes with a guest. We record. We talk. The talk gets transcribed. Then someone has to figure out what is actually worth taking from the conversation into the rest of the work. For each essay on this site, we ask one simple thing: what are the five questions a listener could sit with this week and find different ground under their feet? That is a hard thing to do well. Most of the sector's "key takeaways" sections produce takeaways nobody takes. They produce summaries that close conversations rather than open them. They turn the messiness of a real conversation into a checklist. We try not to do that. The prompts are designed to leave you slightly less settled than when you started. That is the work.

**Where AI fits.** The essays on this site are AI-assisted. So are the prompts. We do not hide that. The note at the top of the data file literally says "AI-generated long-form blog posts." It would be strange not to acknowledge it. What AI is doing: helping turn a fifty-minute conversation into structured long-form text, extracting the underlying questions, suggesting a frame, drafting the prose. It is fast at this. It is a useful tool. What AI is not doing: the conversation, the listening, the choosing of what matters, the willingness to be wrong on the record, the personal stake the three of us carry into each recording. None of that is generated. None of that can be.

> The AI is a tool. The thinking is ours. We are not embarrassed about either part.

There is a temptation in this moment, especially in the humanitarian sector, to either dismiss AI as a corner-cutting trick or to embrace it as a replacement for thinking. We think both moves are wrong. The first is nostalgia. The second is the thing Thomas Jepson-Lay warned about in Episode 7 when he talked about pilots and the autopilot. If you outsource the part of the work that builds the skill, the skill atrophies. You do not notice until the autopilot fails.

So we use AI as a tool. The prompts are not generated live every time someone clicks "Ask me another." They are written, reviewed, and committed to the site once. The button is a rotation through pre-written questions. The AI helped write them. The AI is not asking them. We are asking them. The button is just a way of putting one of them in front of you at a moment when you might let it land.

**What the tool is actually for.** The Pause Button is not a feature. It is not a content strategy. It is a small invitation, repeated. Most of the things in this sector that ask for your attention assume you are going to read them, nod, and move on. The whole architecture of the work is built on volume: more updates, more reports, more meetings, more decks. The Pause Button is the opposite move. It asks you to slow down on one question.

**The sector's AI problem in miniature.** Ali Al Mokdad keeps coming back to a story from Episode 7. He generated twenty-two annexes for a local partner using AI, because the prime applicant requested twenty-two annexes that would never be implemented. AI request, AI response. Documents flowing in both directions. None of them attached to the real work. He called it building an alternative reality. That is what AI as a default tool looks like in this sector right now. It is not the AI's fault. It is what you get when you point a tool that produces content at a system that demands content for its own sake. The Pause Button is a small attempt to point the same tool in the other direction. Less content. More questions. Slower. Not because the question takes more time to read, but because the question takes more time to honestly answer.

**What this is not.** It is not a wellness moment. It is not a "take a deep breath" intervention. It is not coaching. The prompts are not nice. Some of them are intentionally uncomfortable. If you find one that does not bother you at all, that is information. Maybe you have done the work on it already. Maybe you have not let it land yet. It is also not the only thing the AI on this site does. The essays themselves are AI-assisted long-form. The episode summaries are AI-assisted. The blog covers are generated by a small JavaScript function rather than by a designer. There is a layer of structural assistance running underneath the whole site. We are not pretending otherwise. The thing the AI is not doing is the conversation, the choice of which question matters, or the work of actually sitting with the answer. That is yours.

---

### Reflections: The Conversation After the Conversation

Reflections by Ali Al Mokdad · 15 min read · first published on LinkedIn on 19 September 2026 (https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/conversation-after-ali-al-mokdad-ffjve/) · canonical: https://thesectordebrief.com/blog/the-conversation-after-the-conversation/

(Reproduced exactly as written by the author, text and hyperlinks; not an episode essay and not an AI interpretation.)

Five people liked your Short.

Twelve people liked your Short.

Twenty people viewed your video.

You have three new subscribers.

My laptop keeps buzzing. A bar slides in at the corner of the screen, sits there, slides away. Another one behind it.

I don't like notifications. Most apps on my phone are muted. Most on my laptop too. I don't like things entering my rhythm before I have decided I want them there.

I should have muted these too. But I would close the tab, come back an hour later, and the number had moved again. People I had never met, doing something with a conversation I had had with two friends.

So I stopped closing them and started reading them.

Why would somebody give an hour to three people thinking out loud with no conclusion at the end? Why share it? Why subscribe after one episode?

A few days ago, the question got bigger. The counter of the Sector Debrief had passed 100,000 views on YouTube.

Later that day I went looking at the other platforms. Spotify. The website. It reached more than seventy countries.

And then I did the thing I know how to do with a question I cannot answer.

Black coffee. Sticky notes. Papers. A seat in front of a window. Earbuds in.

Thinking. Reflecting.

I started writing.

Looking at the numbers sparks my curiosity. People from different age groups, sectors, cities and parts of the world. Some listening, some watching, some reading transcripts, some translating them. Some watching on TV instead of phones or laptops.

People I know. People I don't. People I will probably never meet.

Numbers become numbers very quickly. This one did not. It sparked curiosity and made me think about the Why.

To understand the why, I have to go back.

I

In October 2024, I gave a webinar called Is the Humanitarian Operational System Reaching Its Expiration Date?

Not exactly the most comforting title.

For a couple of years before that, I had been talking and writing about how we design humanitarian and development programmes, how we run operations, how organisations structure themselves, and why the machinery kept breaking, how the system kept failing the people it promised to serve. I kept seeing things that, to me, looked like symptoms. So I started calling them that. System symptoms. Expiry date symptoms.

The webinar was an attempt to put some of them together. This is what I am seeing. This is what I think is not working. This is why I think it is important to pay so much attention.

Afterwards, people reached out to me through LinkedIn, email and coffee invitations. People I knew. People I didn't. Some were curious. Some challenged the argument. Some wanted the data behind my assessment.

But there was a pattern. A lot of people thought I was exaggerating. Maybe I was frustrated with the sector. Maybe I was pessimistic.

Others were more direct.

Ali, you should stop saying this. It does not help. It will end your career.

It was so strange. People agreed in private but were quiet in public and said something totally different.

It felt like the sector had so many private truths and public lies.

On 25 December 2024, I was invited to speak in another webinar, this time to talk about what I thought might happen next. The hosts were generous enough to give me the space to share my thoughts. I shared what I was seeing. Again, some people thought I was exaggerating.

Then after almost a month came the USAID cuts, and everything that followed.

There is no need to retell that story to people in this sector. We lived it. Projects stopped. Organisations restructured. People lost jobs. Offices closed. Budgets disappeared. The shock moved through organisations, communities and families.

For weeks and months afterwards, people reached out. Some wanted advice. Some wanted to know how I saw that coming. Some wanted to think together. Some wanted a comforting voice or optimistic message.

What stayed with me was something else.

Guilt.

A strange kind of guilt. I had spoken about the limitation, change, the need for transformation. Written about it, presented it, repeated it. But somehow I felt I had failed to make the message go far enough.

Not because I wanted to be right. I would have preferred to be wrong.

But because perhaps some things could have been done earlier. Perhaps we could have changed before change was forced on us.

I went quiet for a while. Thinking. Mapping. Writing. Trying to understand what my role in all of this was. What do I actually want to do? What is useful? What is noise? What do you do when you think you can see something coming but don't know how to make people care about it?

I had been writing another book for two years. I parked it, the manuscript went into a folder I did not open again that year.

And something else came out instead. Quantum Humanitarian. A place to think out loud. Not recommendations. Not action points. Not an executive summary. Just thoughts, frustrations, hope, caring, challenge, contradictions.

Around the same time, the Small c Cut series started taking shape. We talk constantly about Transformation. Big T. Strategies, roadmaps, reorganisations, new operating models. What if, instead, we looked closely at one thing that was not working and made a small cut? Why are we doing this? Does it still make sense? What would happen if we stopped? Small c. No revolution. Just a cut.

The book travelled. The Small c pieces travelled. More invitations came, and most of the time I said yes, sometimes when I probably should have said no, because I thought speaking mattered. And in many ways it worked. I met people. I entered networks. Conversations became projects. Ideas moved.

The more I was invited to speak in events, the more I felt I was speaking and not really having conversations.

There were usually a few questions already prepared. There was an agenda. Often a long introduction. And sometimes, before we started, I was told: maybe don't go too much into this. Probably better not to discuss that. Let's be careful with this one.

Understandable. Organisations have positions. Donors have agendas. People have titles. Institutions have reputations. Communications teams have jobs to do. Political environments have consequences. But layer after layer, something happens. The conversation gets smaller. The more important the issue, the heavier the room. The heavier the room, the more careful the language.

A room with a herd of elephants in it, and all of us talking around them with our eyes closed. I open one to check they are still there. Then I hint.

We work in a sector that talks a lot about courage, but we have also become very good at self-censorship. Sometimes somebody tells us not to speak. Often nobody has to. We do the work ourselves. We edit the sentence before saying it. We calculate. What will my organisation think? What will the donor think? Will someone take one sentence out of context? Will this affect my work? My reputation? My next job? Eventually, everybody can end up saying very reasonable things. And nobody says very much.

I appreciated those events, webinars and podcasts. I still do. But I started craving something else. Not another space where someone had five questions and I had five answers. I wanted to think with someone. I wanted to say something unfinished and hear: maybe. I don't agree. Why? I never thought about it that way. Or simply: I don't know.

I wanted a conversation that did not know where it was going.

And strangely, I was already having those conversations.

II

Around that time, I was engaging with Kim Kucinskas through Humentum transformation initiatives and multiple other working groups focusing on making sense of what happened, building spaces, including some work with the Pledge for Change. I liked those meetings. I looked forward to them. Not because every meeting produced something revolutionary, but because I felt we could think. We could imagine. We could disagree. We could ask what the future might look like without immediately needing to turn that thought into a workplan. They gave me hope sometimes. Not the motivational kind. Just the feeling that there were people genuinely trying to think differently.

I found something similar with Thomas Jepson-Lay. We would have a Pledge for Change conversation. The meeting would finish. And then another conversation would start. The unofficial one. The after-meeting conversation.

We would start with the Pledge, then the sector, then leadership, then systems, then something frustrating, then something hopeful, then something from many years ago, then something that might happen a couple of years from now. Those were often the conversations I thought about and reflected on afterwards.

We seem to share some values. I say seem because I have never sat with Kim and Thomas and tried to write them down. I don't want to. Maybe the fact that they are felt rather than declared is part of what makes the conversations work.

There is trust. There is respect. There is enough safety to disagree. Enough friendship to laugh. Enough experience to know that simple answers to complicated things usually deserve suspicion. And enough curiosity to keep asking the question anyway.

One day, one of those calls with Thomas was ending, and the idea came almost as a joke.

We should record this.

Maybe other people would like to hear it.

Yeah. Maybe.

Who else?

Kim. Kim would be brilliant.

So we emailed her. The subject line was “Recording Our Conversations, would you join us?”

Kim answered: "This sounds like a whole lot of fun. I am around this week for a call if you are."

That was more or less the strategy.

A couple more emails. A Zoom call. Then a recording. Three people. No production team. No content strategy. No audience analysis. No KPI framework. No theory of change. No real idea what we were doing. Not even a proper name. We just talked the same way we were already talking.

Except this time, someone pressed record. What that does to a conversation is a question I am still asking.

Then we needed a logo.

No idea.

There was a painting in Kim’s background.

That looks nice.

My son drew it.

What is it?

A giraffe.

Hmm.

It looks artistic.

Maybe we should use it.

Okay.

So we did.

Then we needed a name. Random words. Debrief kept appearing. The Sector Debrief? Yeah. That sounds fine. Maybe we use that until we figure out what this thing actually is.

A temporary name. A giraffe. Three friends. Zoom.

That was it. We recorded. We published.

A few people shared it. Some wrote things on LinkedIn. We read what they wrote. Then, naturally, some of their comments became part of the next conversation.

About a month later, we recorded again. We went back to something absurdly basic. What is a sector? We talked about it. Recorded it. Published it.

III

Then reality started arriving.

Apparently, when you record something, you have to do things with it afterwards. There is video, audio, editing, descriptions, titles, thumbnails, platforms, uploads, links, websites.

Our WhatsApp group became something between a production team and a governance structure. Should the title be this? Yes, let's do it. What about the description? No, change that bit. It's going live now. We haven't edited this. That's okay, we can do it later. It's live. Someone is asking something. Interesting. Maybe we should talk about that next time.

And we kept going.

Then names started coming. People we admired. People whose thinking we wanted in the room. Aisha. Sofia. Sabrina. Vanessa. Susan and many other leaders.

And then we would look at the calendar. Three busy people. There was always something: travel, work, projects, deadlines, families, life.

So somehow the limitation protected the simplicity. The Sector Debrief remained what it had started as. A place for us to meet, think together and record it. Not because we had designed a minimalist production philosophy. Mostly because we didn't have time for anything else.

We tried better recording software. One was full of bugs and the screen kept flashing black. We tried microphones. Sometimes we used them. Sometimes we forgot.

We never really talked about numbers. We never sat together and asked how we would grow this, or what our target should be. There was just a calendar invitation. When the time came, we clicked. We talked. Afterwards, we downloaded the recording, put the giraffe on it, uploaded it, took out the audio, put that somewhere else and shared it on LinkedIn and WhatsApp groups. Then we went back to whatever else we were doing.

And then I ruined the simplicity slightly, because I couldn't stop myself from playing with it.

At some point, the experiment started moving beyond the conversations themselves.

We had a domain. I started playing with code. One AI agent worked on the website. Another AI agent looked at what the first had done. Others looked at cybersecurity, transcripts, reflections and data. A strange little AI community on the website started growing around three humans having conversations.

My laptop was not consulted about any of this. It froze halfway through a task, filled the screen with insufficient RAM alarm, and asked to be restarted.

Of course, none of those AI agents woke up one morning passionate about humanitarianism or transformation. I was prompting them, giving them a sequence, correcting them, deleting things, getting annoyed, starting again, breaking things and fixing them. But I enjoyed experimenting with it and watching it.

People began using the website. Some read the reflections. Some searched the conversations. Some found us through Google.

And what I liked was that AI was not replacing the part I cared about. It could not replace Kim. It could not replace Thomas. It could not replace the pause when someone is genuinely trying to work out what they think. What it could do was carry some of the weight around the administrative part of our conversations.

IV

Why?

I don't know. And I don't want to pretend that I do.

Some of those notifications are about Shorts. The thing I care about is an hour of three people thinking.

I still want people to pay attention to what I think I can see coming. I also want a conversation that does not know where it is going. I have not worked out how those two fit together.

I enjoy listening to Kim and Thomas think. I enjoy changing my own mind halfway through a sentence.

Maybe people hear something that sounds like the conversation they have with a colleague after everyone else has left the meeting. That conversation. The one after the conversation. The thing you say once the presentation is closed. Once the donor has left. Once the minutes are finished. Once nobody is taking notes.

Our sector has no shortage of places for finished thinking: panels, reports, strategies, keynotes, position papers, guidance, recommendations, talking points, launches. We have fewer places for thinking itself. For I don't know. For I used to think that, but I am not sure any more. For somebody to change their mind in public. For people to speak for an hour without representing an organisation. For leadership vulnerability.

Does a hundred thousand views prove there is an appetite for that? No. I don't think numbers prove things that neatly.

V

There is an irony in all of this.

If The Sector Debrief keeps growing, perhaps one day we will have to protect it from becoming the thing that made us want to create it. More people. More expectations. More structure. Maybe resources. Maybe partners. Maybe more hosts. Maybe summits. Maybe different languages. Maybe funding. Maybe sponsors.

We keep asking ourselves what we want from it. What is the objective? What outcome are we trying to achieve? How will we measure it? Which is a very sector question. And maybe somebody will suggest a strategic planning retreat. Hopefully not too soon.

Because growth creates weight, and the things it would press on are small. Three busy people. A calendar invitation. The freedom to say I don't know.

There is also something I have no answer to. Every sentence we say can be replayed later by an employer, a donor, a future recruiter. The calculation I described earlier applies to us as much as to anyone. Friendship among three people makes it easier for the three of us. It does not make it safe for anyone else who might want to speak the same way.

But in the end, it is about better questions, not faster answers, and I keep asking myself questions.

How do you become bigger without becoming heavier?

How do you keep saying I don't know when people start expecting you to know?

Maybe that is where Small c comes back into my life again. Build what is needed. Cut what gets in the way. Keep the machinery light. Protect the human part. Don't turn the means into the purpose. And leave some things unfinished.

VI

People viewed your video. People liked your Short. You have new subscribers.

My laptop still gives me those notifications. I still don't like them. I still don't like the sound. I still don't particularly like something deciding that it deserves my attention.

But every now and then, I look.

Not because I need to know whether the number went up.

Because somewhere behind that notification is a person. Someone watching on a TV. Someone reading a transcript in another language. Someone who agrees. Someone who thinks we are completely wrong. Someone who heard something and stayed for another few minutes. People.

A view might not be a person and might not mean people watched the full hour of our conversation. But people wrote about us, listened to us. They entered something that had started between three people who wanted to think and reflect out loud. By watching, by listening, by writing, by sharing.

And somewhere in that journey, something that began as ours became slightly less ours.

What will The Sector Debrief become? I really don't know. For now, a living experiment. It gives us joy. It makes us think. And apparently, something about it makes other people stay around too.

For now, I think that is enough.

Ali Al Mokdad

---

### Essay: If Not Us, Then Who? A Moral Story

Companion to Episode 14 · 9 min read · canonical: https://thesectordebrief.com/blog/if-not-us-then-who/

(A note on method, stated in the essay itself: this is the hosts' reading of the conversation, drafted from the episode transcript. The quoted passages are as spoken on camera; everything else is interpretation.)

Kim Kucinskas, Thomas Jepson-Lay and Ali Al Mokdad were joined by Yuriy Boyechko, who introduced himself as the CEO and founder of Hope for Ukraine and the author of a forthcoming book, Defiant Hope: Ordinary Lives, Extraordinary Courage, and the Fight for Ukraine. Hope for Ukraine has worked on the ground in Ukraine since 2016 and marks ten years this year. He described food distribution through a family support programme, a solar energy resilience programme, five other programmes, about 1,500 volunteers working with them every day, a headquarters in Roseland, New Jersey, and a humanitarian hub in Lviv. When he left, the microphones stayed on for a Hot Debrief.

Operations Is the Impact.

Ali opened with the numbers he had found on the organisation's website: revenue of a little over $5 million, around 90% of it going to direct programme costs, and millions of people reached. How, he asked, does an organisation that size reach that many people? Yuriy's first answer was short.

As spoken on camera: "Because we look at spreadsheets every morning."

He then listed what sits behind it. Volunteers, because paying everyone who does the work on the ground would make the costs balloon. Vendors reassessed almost every week. Food that was bought in Europe at the start of the war and is now bought from producers in Ukraine, which he said roughly halved the cost. A shipping deal with one logistics company in the United States that also lets them store goods and build containers in its facility. His estimate was that $5 million does something like $20 million worth of work on the ground. Kim recognised her own field in it: this, she said, is the intersection between impact and operations, and in technical language much of it is cost share.

A Delivery App for Aid.

Kim asked how the logistics and the people are kept running, and Yuriy's answer was technology. In 2024 he had the idea of something like DoorDash for humanitarian aid, after seeing pictures of long lines of people waiting with paperwork, and distributions that took hours because of the strict documentation required on the Ukrainian side. After two vendors, they built the app and launched it at the beginning of 2025. Partners register and are verified, goods move from the warehouse to a partner, the partner creates a distribution event that shows on a map and a calendar, and the report comes back with pictures. Everything, he said, is visible in real time, work that would otherwise take about three people.

When the System Rolled In.

Thomas described, as he put it, an outside narrative from someone who has never worked in Ukraine: an international system that arrived with the same processes it uses everywhere, and rolled out a localisation process alongside it at the same time. Yuriy's account began in 2022, when every NGO came, and went on to 2024, when many left. The reason he gave was a new government rule after a year of waste: once aid crosses the border, the organisation on the ground has 90 days to document where it went and who received it. His example was a hospital in the Mykolaiv region that was brought a commercial generator by a well-meaning partner abroad and already had seven of them in the backyard.

Hope for Ukraine could not leave, he said, because it is a Ukraine-based organisation, so it hired a legal team and local Ukrainian counsel and built the infrastructure to work with the government, and then built the app on top of it. He described the approach as grassroots up rather than top down: before a team is deployed, the person driving the van is the one who says whether a road is safe. And after USAID was dismantled, he said, the old model of an office in Washington and a report once a year is over.

Innovate or Go Out of Business.

Ali asked whether the experimenting was designed into the organisation or came from need. Yuriy said it was intentional, and traced it to his earlier career in media and entertainment, pitching reality shows. 2022 was a good year for everyone. In 2023 their revenue dropped 75% in one year.

As spoken on camera: "So in 2023, it was the point where I realized we either innovate or we just go out of business as an organization."

What followed, in his account, was updates on social media every two hours, a growing donor base, the app, and this year a tool built with the same developers that uses AI to match their programmes with open funding opportunities, with a person verifying and applying. The book, he said, is meant to work as a development tool too, sitting on shelves around the world. Later in the conversation he put a number on the change: since the bad year of 2023, the organisation has grown 70% to 100% year over year.

If Not Us, Then Who?

Thomas asked how a leader works with hope, and with a base of volunteers. Yuriy spoke about volunteers who have been with them since the start of the full-scale war, some of whom have made 157 trips to the front line, unpaid, with a van full of goods and a tank full of gas. He lives, he said, by one phrase: communication is the lifeline of every relationship. Then he told the story of Natalia, who works for them in Kherson. She has lost her home to occupation, her father and her husband, and lives in the city with her 14-year-old son, under constant drone attack. He has told her she could take her son and move somewhere peaceful.

As spoken on camera: "And she always gives me the same answer: if not us, then who?"

There are 60,000 people still living in the town, she tells him, mostly elderly and sick, and she will stay as long as there are supplies to distribute. Yuriy's own word for what that does to others was contagious: people write and call every week from Australia, New Zealand, Britain and the United States asking to volunteer on the ground. That, he said, is defiant hope.

Scale or Replicate.

Kim said her mind kept going to scale and that she was uncomfortable with it, because maybe not everything needs to be scaled. Yuriy described a foundation built through trial and error on two pillars, technology and a grassroots movement. They distribute about 2,000 food kits a week and could distribute 4,000 if there were money for the food, because the people on the ground are ready. Their average donation is $50, from thousands of donors he calls owners. Their office policy is that every email is answered and every phone call returned within 24 hours. At a donor roundtable, one person told them they read every one of the emails that go out twice a week.

Thomas drew a line between two ideas that often get merged.

As spoken on camera: "Now, for me, there's a strong distinction between scale and replicability."

Yuriy's answer was a system that can be adjusted in days rather than weeks, attention on the most critical need of the community, and an organisation that can explain what it does in one sentence, because, as he put it, the public votes with money.

Energy as Assistance.

Ali asked about the solar programme, which he saw as energy as assistance, a type of programming that sits between humanitarian and development work. Yuriy described families who had food kits but nothing to cook on, firewood deliveries, and open fires close to the front line whose smoke could bring a drone. One day in a Costco he saw a solar power generator, bought one with a panel and a cooktop, and tested it. They first bought units store by store around New Jersey and now have a direct supplier. The programme, he said, was nominated this year for the Reuters Sustainability Awards alongside multi-billion-dollar companies. A pets programme followed this year, using the vans that come back empty from the front line to move abandoned dogs and cats to shelters.

As spoken on camera: "I think the revenue will follow impact, not vision casting."

Asked about his own experience of the full-scale invasion, Yuriy said that a lot of his family is still there, his father among them, and kept the answer short.

A Moral Story.

Ali named what he had been hearing.

As spoken on camera: "The story that I'm hearing, for me, it's not the classic story. It's a moral story."

It is about solidarity, innovation, experimenting and resilience, he said, and it is the kind of story the sector should tell more: values and principles shown in practice, rather than only needs and struggles. In the Hot Debrief Kim said she had been in listening mode the whole time, and that the way Yuriy speaks makes complex things seem obvious.

As spoken on camera: "This is how development should just be done."

Thomas wished he had asked whether anyone from the multilateral system had sat down with Yuriy and asked how things work there. He was careful about taking the model and copying it elsewhere: it works, in his view, because it is a local organisation in its own context, and the question for the international system is what support it can bring to something like this. For him the mission Yuriy narrated was values-based.

As spoken on camera: "Building hope was his mission."

Ali named three things he would keep thinking about: numbers that back up the story, energy treated as an essential need, and the moral story itself. Kim described a business as usual that is itself innovation, meant to meet tomorrow's need, and asked what the universal lessons are: technology meeting people, values as a spine, and communication that is clear. She ended on the role of intermediaries, and on why that unglamorous work needs to be funded in a different way. Thomas added the role international organisations can play in raising the profile of crises that are off the radar, and the conversation ended there, as a topic for the next episode.

A note on these notes, because this page promises honesty about how it is made. This essay is our reading of the conversation, drafted from the episode transcript. The quoted passages are as spoken on camera. Everything else is interpretation, and that interpretation is ours. The episode itself, including the Hot Debrief, is the place to hear it in full.

### Essay: Tell Me What to Stop. The Justification Fatigue

Companion to Episode 13 · 11 min read · canonical: https://thesectordebrief.com/blog/tell-me-what-to-stop/

(A note on method, stated in the essay itself: this is the hosts' reading of the conversation, drafted from the episode transcript. The quoted passages are as spoken on camera; everything else is interpretation.)

This was the first episode recorded without Ali, and Kim Kucinskas and Thomas Jepson-Lay were joined by Ahmed Ibrahim. He introduced himself with close to twenty years in the NGO world in East Africa, most of it in Somalia, with time in South Sudan, Sudan, Kenya and Ethiopia and briefly in Rwanda and Burundi, and a career that has run through the UN, international organisations, consultancies of his own and other people's, universities, and government work as a consultant. The conversation was about leading through the cuts, seen from the place where the decisions made in headquarters meet the work in the field. When he left, the microphones stayed on for a Hot Debrief. Both halves are in the episode.

Then and Now.

Thomas asked how the turbulence in the world looks from East Africa now, compared with twenty years ago. Ahmed started in late 2006, which he remembers as the peak of the world's interest in the region. In 2007, he said, close to a quarter of a million people were displaced outside Mogadishu, and the question was never how much money there was, only who could deliver the water and where it could be taken. Now, by his account, less than 10% of the resources that used to reach that part of the world are available, while the number of internally displaced people in Somalia has gone from less than half a million to more than three million. Attention has moved as well, to Ukraine, to Sudan, to Gaza and the Middle East.

As spoken on camera: "People talk about donor fatigue, which has been a very popular word for a while, but I can tell you we have the justification fatigue."

He put change fatigue next to it: a structure built today, a cut five months later and a new structure, another cut three months after that and another structure, until people are tired enough to ask whether it would be better to stop altogether. Many organisations, he said, already have. What worries him most is the ambiguity of what comes next.

Cutting from the Bottom Up.

Thomas heard in that picture a system that had made the region dependent on multilateral aid, and asked whether anything new is growing in the gap it leaves. Ahmed described two patterns instead. The first is how organisations shrink: from the lowest level, not the highest. The field offices close first, everyone moves to the country office, and the organisation loses its connection with the communities it serves. The people who make the decisions keep their own posts until last, and he did not exclude himself from that. What remains can be a big skeleton of directors with less technical capacity under them.

The second is localisation. If international organisations are too big and their machinery too expensive, the money and the capacity should move to smaller local organisations that can do the work. In his assessment the opposite is happening: the large organisations need to survive, so they transfer less. And when USAID closed, he said, the shock spread quickly to the other donors in the region, and offices closed and left communities without a proper transition. Where he sits, the argument now is for prevention rather than response, because responding to everyone will not be possible.

Tell Me What to Stop.

Kim said that listening to him made her feel exhausted, and asked the question underneath the strategy: how is he doing, and how are his peers doing, in a position that pulls from both ends? Ahmed answered with the arithmetic of it. A team of ten becomes five, and the five who remain take on the work of the five who left. At the same moment the global office expects more money to be raised, at a time when it is very difficult to raise it, and more impact to be shown from less. The person who links the field to the global office absorbs the shocks from below and the pressure from above. The tool he described came from a conversation with a supervisor:

As spoken on camera: "when you ask me do more on this, tell me also what I need to stop."

Otherwise, he said, he inherits crisis, and ends up frustrated and exhausted, or leaves. So the questions become which reports and which meetings could stop, and whether there is room for creative thinking at all, because an overwhelmed person stops thinking and only responds. Kim finished the sentence for him.

As spoken on camera: "You're putting out fires and there's no oxygen to reflect."

Thomas recognised the pattern from the time he and Ahmed worked together: everyone agreed in principle that you cannot do more with less, and everyone was on board with dropping something until it came to their own thing. In his work with leadership teams now he hears something more: decisions arriving from more senior people without much explanation, and people experiencing them as an assault on their personal value. The hurt and the firefighting compound each other, he said, and the result is that people repeat what they have done before.

Strategy and the Back Office.

Asked about the challenges he faces as a leader, Ahmed separated two lines that rarely meet. Organisations are quick to adapt their vision, strategy, plans and priorities. Their bureaucracy, operational guidelines and policies do not move with them, and the people in operations, finance and human resources are left outside the shift. His example was localisation itself: the commitment is in the strategy, but it is not clear what it means for the partnership department, and a finance director whose concern is to cover operating costs and a technical team that wants to transfer more to local partners end up pulling against each other. The work, as he described it, is convergence between the thinking and the delivery.

He added two more. A single incident, poor performance or misuse of resources in one far-away office, can turn quickly into a new rule for everyone, at exactly the moment when there are fewer people and fewer resources. And genuine failure has to be allowed. If the smallest failure has negative consequences, nobody will take the risks that a resource crisis demands.

Kim laughed, because this is her day-to-day: the intersection of big ideas and what she now calls strategic operations. Locally led development, she said, eventually hits a finance manager or a compliance officer who has to absorb it as part of their own values and be willing to give something up.

As spoken on camera: "Because you don't get to accompany and be in solidarity with if you are not giving up something."

Ahmed's answer was that the change has to belong to the whole organisation rather than one department, that operational and bureaucratic approaches have to become as adaptive as the thinking, and that the people who rarely leave the building should be taken out of the rooms to see the forces driving the change, rather than written off as difficult.

When Values Clash.

Kim named the harder version. When money was flowing, an organisation could usually find alignment between how it needed to run and meeting the mission. When money becomes scarce, two values can be at odds: the programmatic impact, and taking care of your own people and keeping the organisation sustainable. Sometimes, she said, the honest move is to call it out and say that trade-offs are coming, and that takes courage and clarity.

Thomas had quite a lot to say about this, by his own announcement. He distinguishes alignment, whether finance, operations and leadership decisions all contribute to the outcomes, from attunement: emotional connectivity and trust across departments, not only within a team. Where attunement exists, he argued, a difficult conversation is still hard, but it can be held. Holding it is a leadership skill, and not one he thinks is widely available at senior level. There is no template for this moment, and blaming the donor is a way of making the organisation a victim of its own decisions. The executive orders, in his reading, were the trigger and not the cause: everything people are now being forced to change already needed changing.

As spoken on camera: "Many, many, many leaders know the language of change. They know the language that they're supposed to say. They understand the rhetoric that is supposed to come out. Their actions don't back it up."

Teams pick that up, he said, and it creates hesitancy, a chilling effect, and people who will not put themselves out there, be creative or fail fast. His remedy was depth reflection by leaders, often helped by a conversation with someone else, whether a partner, a trusted colleague, a peer or a coach.

Trust Is Expensive.

Ahmed remembered a forum where Thomas asked what was going right and what was going wrong, and some colleagues answered that everything was going right. Thomas's reply, as Ahmed recalled it, was that in that case they did not need the meeting. The defensiveness, Ahmed said, is the thing to change: asking whether there is a better way of working is not an attack. He described asking a boss for the two big things the office should achieve, hearing that the first was to mobilise resources, and asking in return why the resources were needed and what they were for.

Kim drew the thread together around attunement, and then around trust. She shared a definition she had heard at a recent conference session, trust as sincerity, reliability, care, competence and safety, and pointed out how much a leader has to demonstrate at once, in actions as well as words. To her, Ahmed's role in the middle means facilitating that attunement whether he wanted the job or not, and doing the emotional labour of code switching, which, she pointed out, is not in his job description.

As spoken on camera: "I actually learned that trust is expensive."

With even a little doubt, Ahmed said, no matter how hard you work, it will always look ugly. Trust starts with your own people, and he described it as psychological safety: the room to say that a decision was wrong, and a leader who can answer that he was wrong and apologise. Then he came back to justification fatigue, which, in his telling, means being asked ten times to explain the same small thing, until you decide not to bring anything new next time, because one small solution costs so much time and energy that you can only afford to bring what is necessary.

Reflections.

Ahmed apologised for getting emotional, and said that people going through this need a place to come together, breathe and share their thinking, even outside the institutions they work in. Kim took away two words, attunement and justification fatigue, and named the opposite of the fatigue as creativity and curiosity, which nobody can offer if they are burnt out by the grind of the system. Thomas challenged the idea of a trade-off, because it turns into a zero-sum framing, and offered discernment instead: understanding where trust sits in the organisation, building it where it does not, owning your own part, and not being a victim in all this.

The Hot Debrief.

After Ahmed left, Kim said she heard the same through lines as in a year of these conversations, in a different context and a different voice. Thomas noted that Ahmed had been careful to stay away from examples that could give organisational details away, which he thought was fair. Kim said she felt the middle role in her own body, and recalled how often the person in that seat is the one in the room asking what it is all for and what about the people.

Thomas connected it to something he kept hearing in the region: we do not want to bother them, they are overworked. He understands the sentiment, but the result, as he described it, is that people at that level are left with business as usual and the performance indicators and excluded from the conversations where something new could happen. Kim had brought up the pole exercise from the last episode, and he returned to it: the task is to lower the pole, and all the noise is about raising it. Kim asked what would happen if the noise were put down, the reporting streamlined and the justification made less exhausting. Thomas described a workshop, five storeys underground in a hotel basement with the fire alarm going off, where he had argued for flipping the demand for data so that it serves the country office's own decisions first and global aggregation second. Kim added learning that runs horizontally, country office to country office, and the possibility of using technology to take some of the noise away.

Thomas also named the question he did not get to ask: in five, ten or twenty years, where will the acts of humanity come from, and what role will leadership at the level of society play, if the answer turns out to be the culmination of many small things rather than the rollout of something big. He suggested they might have to have Ahmed back to ask it. Kim noted that this was the first time they had recorded without Ali and said they would be interested to hear his thoughts, and Thomas suggested starting the next episode with them.

A note on these notes, because this page promises honesty about how it is made. This essay is our reading of the conversation, drafted from the episode transcript. The quoted passages are as spoken on camera. Everything else is interpretation, and that interpretation is ours. The episode itself, including the Hot Debrief, is the place to hear it in full.

---

### Essay: The Words and the Work. Acting, or Acting?

Companion to Episode 12 · 11 min read · canonical: https://thesectordebrief.com/blog/the-words-and-the-work/

(A note on method, stated in the essay itself: this is the hosts' reading of the conversation, drafted from the episode transcript. The quoted passages are as spoken on camera; everything else is interpretation.)

This one had no guest. Kim Kucinskas, Thomas Jepson-Lay, and Ali Al Mokdad sat down to freestyle, and Thomas opened with a question for Kim: why was it taking her so long to make sense of the conference season? Her answer was three conferences in two weeks, the UNGA side events in New York, the WINGS Forum in Montreal, and two days at the InterAction Annual Conference in Washington, D.C., and a book of notes she expected to turn around on the Monday. Three weeks later it was still settling. What follows is our reading of where that took the three of us.

Same Words in Every Room.

Kim's first headline was the vocabulary. Trust, solidarity, collaboration, humility: the same words across all three events, used in different ways. She admitted to feeling angsty and grumpy about it at first, because the sector has been using these words for decades, and without action behind them they become, in her phrase, kind of words. Then a line from the opening of the WINGS Forum, whose theme was act, gave her a frame for it.

As spoken on camera: "You can take action and do something, or you can be an actor in a performance."

That is the question the episode keeps returning to. When we say these words, are we walking the talk, or performing a part we think we are supposed to play? Kim was careful to call it a spectrum rather than all or nothing, with a lot of good intent in the middle that does not always lead to action. Where she has run out of patience is the performance. And she located the difference in small decisions rather than big gestures: how do I trust by being trustworthy, how do I collaborate elbows down instead of talking about the importance of collaboration. Those, she said, add up.

She also described three different angles on the same words. At UNGA the conversation was still diagnosing how institutions built 80 years ago are holding up. At WINGS, philanthropy was in a reform-or-die mood. At InterAction, among mainly US-based INGOs, it was still largely protect mode. Her point was that each room tends to think its reality is the reality, and that the sector needs a more coherent way of talking about itself even where people disagree on tactics.

Words That Do Not Translate.

Ali had the same experience in Brussels the month before: the same messages, the same talking points, the same words, including from donors. He added a test of his own. When he works in another language, much of this vocabulary does not carry over; the words sound vague and cloudy, sometimes naive, and he finds he has to describe what they would look like in practice before they mean anything.

As spoken on camera: "No, it's even like when you want to just talk about them in different language, they just don't have a meaning."

Thomas, who described himself as only an English speaker after years in rooms where he did not understand the language being spoken, noted that the terminology of the multilateral sector arrives in English anyway: a whole paragraph in another language can still carry terms like the cluster system. For him it shows how Westernised the system is. Read together, the two points make a useful check for any of these words: if a term only works in the language it was coined in, it may be describing a posture rather than a practice.

A Shift in the Language.

Thomas pushed on whether anything was actually different this year, since the same reflections could carry almost any date. Kim's honest answer started with her notebook: flipping through it, she found pages she took to be from this event that were dated nine months earlier. She also offered a caveat we think is worth keeping. There is no such thing as a trend, only the signals you are listening for, and the sessions she attended and the notes she took reflect her own perspective.

With that caveat, she did hear a difference in posture. Philanthropy, in her account, was asking whether to get rid of the grant system or one-year grants altogether, and locally led development and shift the power were no longer being argued for at WINGS because they were already assumed. And she heard the language moving: solidarity, humanity, and collaboration, rather than the technical vocabulary of efficiency, effectiveness, and risk. Underneath it, she said, is a set of values the sector assumed 80 years ago and has not kept refreshing.

As spoken on camera: "But if you don't really defend this kind of humanistic set of values as a spine to everything you do, then the alternative is someone else is going to replace it with a different set of values."

Thomas called that move, from managerialist language of measurement and cost to relational and values-based language, an important pivot he had not heard called out before. Kim added the counterweight: in other rooms the language was still country first, and not only in America.

An NGO Class, and Everything Outside the Sector.

Ali then offered three thoughts, which he framed as thinking aloud rather than conclusions. The first was a question about whether the sector has created, at country level, a class of its own: well paid, a little elite, with its own coffee shops, its own places, and its own language, living in the abstract in a way that does not match the communities around it. He raised it from what he saw in the countries where he has worked. The second was the vocabulary again.

As spoken on camera: "So are we just getting very good at adapting terminology, but not behaviour and practice?"

Each period brings a new set of terms, he said, sometimes recycled ones, and at least for funding that has worked before. The third came from a survey that asked what was happening outside the sector. His answer was everything: the economy, debt and credit, geopolitics, climate, innovation. The sector is part of a larger ecosystem, not its centre. And much of the funding for international aid and development is taxpayers' money, which follows decisions people made when they voted. Changing the language after each cut, in his view, is not the same as being proactive. Thomas recommended the book Dull Disasters, co-written by the former DFID economist Stefan Dercon, which in his reading makes the same point: aid finance follows votes and how the public perceives the cause.

Warm Connections, and Nothing Done With Them.

Thomas brought the conversation home to Somerset, where he had spent the day before in two conversations about community resilience. Everyone agreed on the problem: economically deprived areas that need an uplift. Everyone was well connected: education, health, emergency services, the council, faith groups, local business, all warmly in touch. And nothing was coming of it beyond nice chats.

As spoken on camera: "you need the connectivity in the relational element but you also then need the action to go along with that."

Kim's reply was that collaboration is a discipline and a skill set, not just an aspiration and a hope, and that it needs to be recognised, resourced, and built. She also brought back two things from the conferences: the growing role of middle actors, from middle states to companies and high net worth individuals, and the number of people who named tax reform as the single change that would matter most. And she connected it to where our previous episode ended, with Thomas and Kim disagreeing about whether the problem is structural or psychological. Real change costs something, she said, and saying the right things is easier than letting it cost you.

Comfortable With Change, or Familiar With It?

Thomas answered with a phrase about taking pleasure in our own displeasure: we are more comfortable bemoaning what we know does not work than moving into a place of unknown discomfort. Then he turned it on leaders.

As spoken on camera: "are you actually comfortable with change or are you just familiar with running change processes? Because those are two very different things."

Ali's view from two to three years of transformation work was that it is a mix. Sometimes knowledge and organisational history are the barrier. Sometimes we forget that organisations are people with their own worries and rhythms. Sometimes the structure itself, field, country, region, headquarters, working groups, task forces, makes a decision almost impossible, and consultation turns into a loop that never produces one. His sharpest example was a simple workflow he had designed, and the comments that came back defending roles rather than improving the flow.

Thomas had a more hopeful signal. Three organisations he is working with, unconnected to each other, have each told him that their current leadership dynamic is not working. He also shared a framing he had heard and found articulate: organisations are comfortable with inherited uncertainty, the context and the environment, and hugely uncomfortable with internal ambiguity, in structure, strategy, trust, culture, and the contradictions between the language of leadership and its actions. That, he said, is where the friction comes from.

When No Choice Is Risk-Free.

Kim then contradicted her own position from the last episode, and said so. Systems are made of people, she agreed, and social change has to come through individual transformation first, which takes a long time. She described a question Nana from WACSI put to a panel, and a session at InterAction on crucible moments, the decisions that forge you through hardship.

As spoken on camera: "When there is no risk-free choice, how do you act?"

Her favourite answer from that week was to pick the side that is best for humanity. Ali added the view from the other side of the funding relationship. In his meetings with donors in Brussels, he found them restructuring, shifting focus, and carrying their own organisational and personal shocks. He felt he was doing emotional support before any conversation, and asked the sector to remember that there are people on the other side too.

The Pole Goes Up.

Thomas then described an exercise from a two-day workshop on collaboration. People line up facing each other with their fingers out, a pole is laid across their fingers, and the task is to lower it to the floor while everyone keeps contact the whole time. Every time, the pole goes up. Everyone assumes someone else is pushing it, because they are not. And every instruction, keep your finger on the pole, keep your finger on it, points up while the task points down. He asked how much of our daily noise works against the direction we say we want to go.

The group did get it down eventually, he said, by attuning: defaulting to one calm voice, moving with one person's breathing, noticing what worked, until the progress fed itself. Kim recognised the sector's vocabulary in it, collective sense making and an abundance mindset, and here was what they look like in practice. Thomas added his ecosystem picture, a single person surrounded by family, neighbours, community, faith groups, diaspora, the private sector, government, and somewhere in there the aid sector, which tends to assume it is all of it. When Kim wondered how attunement could scale globally, and offered humanity as the common denominator, Thomas added this.

As spoken on camera: "It's not the rollout of big, it's the culmination of small."

Money and Moral Purpose.

Thomas did not want the episode to end on a simple moral, and he spoke directly to boards and executives. The need for financial stability is real, and so is the pressure to grow and compete for money. The biggest leadership challenge, in his words, is keeping the balance, and with a million surplus, whatever you decide, you will be criticised for it. Kim's response was that when values compete, you either make a transparent decision and feel okay about it, or you find the balance. Thomas added that there is no off-the-shelf answer and precedent is increasingly irrelevant: the leaders thriving now are the ones stepping out of known displeasures into unknown discomforts. Ali was candid that inside the machine he is driven by the same numbers, and that conversations like this one are what let him step back and balance them. Kim credited Thomas with the discernment and the pause, and Thomas noted that we do not budget for time.

Where We Left It.

Kim left with more clarity, and with a mix of same old, same old and a little optimism. Ali left with a reminder that systems and institutions are people, and that those on the other side are struggling too. Thomas left with the two meanings of act, the performance and the progress. Kim had the last word.

As spoken on camera: "Am I acting or am I acting?"

A note on these notes, because this page promises honesty about how it is made. This essay is our reading of the conversation, drafted from the episode transcript. The quoted passages are as spoken on camera. Everything else is interpretation, and that interpretation is ours. The episode itself is the place to hear it in full.
